igcse-0580-operations-signed.description: Follow changes across zero and determine the sign of a product or quotient.

sections.title: Which way should I move?
sections.label: Directions
sections.intro: A positive change moves to the right on a horizontal number line. A negative change moves to the left. Start at the first number and count the change from there.

blocks.html: Draw a short number line for temperatures or levels crossing zero.

figure.alt: Number line from minus four to plus three, with a right arrow between them.
figure.caption: A rise of 7 moves from minus 4 through zero to 3.

blocks.prompt: A store room starts at \(-11\) °C. Its temperature rises by 23 °C. What is its new temperature?
blocks.hint: Start below zero and take the rise to the right.
blocks.solution:
Start at \(-11\) and move right by 23 because the temperature rises.

Use 11 of those steps to reach zero. There are 12 steps left.

The calculation is \(-11+23=12\). The new temperature is 12 °C.

retry.feedback: The starting temperature is negative. First count the steps needed to reach zero.

blocks.html: A rise changes the temperature by the given amount. It does not give the final temperature directly.

blocks.prompt: A store room starts at \(-14\) °C. Its temperature rises by 29 °C. What is its new temperature?
blocks.hint: Start below zero and take the rise to the right.
blocks.solution:
Start at \(-14\) and move right by 29 because the temperature rises.

Use 14 of those steps to reach zero. There are 15 steps left.

The calculation is \(-14+29=15\). The new temperature is 15 °C.

retry.feedback: The starting temperature is negative. First count the steps needed to reach zero.

sections.title: What does subtracting a negative do?
sections.label: Subtracting
sections.intro: A negative number tells you a direction. Subtracting that number reverses that direction.

blocks.html: Subtract a negative by adding its positive opposite.

blocks.hint: Subtracting a negative moves right on the number line.
blocks.solution:
Subtracting \(-23\) reverses the effect of adding \(-23\).

Replace the subtraction of a negative by addition: \(-11+23\).

The value is \(12\).

retry.feedback: This is the result of adding a negative number. The question subtracts it.

blocks.html: Keep the sign on the starting value. Only the operation with the second value changes.

blocks.hint: Subtracting a negative moves right on the number line.
blocks.solution:
Subtracting \(-29\) reverses the effect of adding \(-29\).

Replace the subtraction of a negative by addition: \(-14+29\).

The value is \(15\).

retry.feedback: This is the result of adding a negative number. The question subtracts it.

sections.title: How can I tell the sign before calculating?
sections.label: Products
sections.intro: For a product or a quotient, deal with the two signs first. Then calculate using the positive magnitudes.

blocks.html: Same signs give positive. Different signs give negative.

blocks.hint: Same signs give a positive result. Different signs give a negative result.
blocks.solution:
Only one factor is negative, so the product is negative.

On the magnitudes, multiply: \(3\times 9=27\).

Put the sign back to obtain \(-27\).

retry.feedback: The magnitude is right. Check how many of the two numbers are negative.

blocks.html: The rule about matching signs is for multiplication and division. Addition and subtraction use the size and direction of changes.

blocks.hint: Same signs give a positive result. Different signs give a negative result.
blocks.solution:
Both numbers are negative, so the quotient is positive.

On the magnitudes, divide: \(60\div 6=10\).

Put the sign back to obtain \(10\).

retry.feedback: The magnitude is right. Check how many of the two numbers are negative.

examples.title: Calculate a signed temperature change
examples.question: A store room starts at \(-4\) °C. Its temperature rises by 9 °C. What is its new temperature?
solution: Start at \(-4\) and move right by 9 because the temperature rises.
Use 4 of those steps to reach zero. There are 5 steps left.
The calculation is \(-4+9=5\). The new temperature is 5 °C.

examples.title: Calculate a signed temperature change
examples.question: A store room starts at \(-7\) °C. Its temperature rises by 15 °C. What is its new temperature?
solution: Start at \(-7\) and move right by 15 because the temperature rises.
Use 7 of those steps to reach zero. There are 8 steps left.
The calculation is \(-7+15=8\). The new temperature is 8 °C.

examples.title: Subtract a negative number
examples.question: Work out \(-4-(-9)\) without a calculator.
solution: Subtracting \(-9\) reverses the effect of adding \(-9\).
Replace the subtraction of a negative by addition: \(-4+9\).
The value is \(5\).

examples.title: Subtract a negative number
examples.question: Work out \(-7-(-15)\) without a calculator.
solution: Subtracting \(-15\) reverses the effect of adding \(-15\).
Replace the subtraction of a negative by addition: \(-7+15\).
The value is \(8\).

examples.title: Decide the sign of a product or quotient
examples.question: Work out \((-30)\div(-6)\) without a calculator.
solution: Both numbers are negative, so the quotient is positive.
On the magnitudes, divide: \(30\div 6=5\).
Put the sign back to obtain \(5\).

examples.title: Decide the sign of a product or quotient
examples.question: Work out \((-9)\times 7\) without a calculator.
solution: Only one factor is negative, so the product is negative.
On the magnitudes, multiply: \(9\times 7=63\).
Put the sign back to obtain \(-63\).

igcse-0580-operations-decimal-add-subtra.description: Align place values before adding or subtracting amounts, lengths and prices.

sections.title: Why should the decimal points line up?
sections.label: Align
sections.intro: Temporarily give the numbers the same smallest place value. This lets you add equal-sized units, such as hundredths.

blocks.html:
Line up the units columns, then the tenths and hundredths. Append zeros where needed.

UnitsDecimal pointTenthsHundredths
6.80
2.07

The missing hundredths digit in the first row is zero.

blocks.hint: Use a zero in a missing hundredths place before adding.
blocks.solution:
Line up the decimal points. Put tenths below tenths and hundredths below hundredths.

Write both numbers as hundredths: 720 and 207. Add these as whole numbers.

The sum is 927 hundredths, or \(9.27\).

blocks.html: Adding a zero at the end of the fractional part keeps the value unchanged. Moving the decimal point changes it.

blocks.hint: Use a zero in a missing hundredths place before adding.
blocks.solution:
Line up the decimal points. Put tenths below tenths and hundredths below hundredths.

Write both numbers as hundredths: 870 and 231. Add these as whole numbers.

The sum is 1101 hundredths, or \(11.01\).

sections.title: What if a column is empty?
sections.label: Exchange
sections.intro: Write a zero so you can see where the missing digit would sit. If needed, exchange one tenth for ten hundredths before subtracting.

blocks.html: Subtraction keeps the same place values in both rows.

blocks.hint: You can subtract using hundredths as the unit. Write a zero in a blank place.
blocks.solution:
Write \(10.20\) so the hundredths are visible.

Subtract 220 hundredths from 1020 hundredths.

800 hundredths is \(8\).

blocks.html: Start at the smallest place. Regroup from the next place to the left if needed.

blocks.hint: You can subtract using hundredths as the unit. Write a zero in a blank place.
blocks.solution:
Write \(12.00\) so the hundredths are visible.

Subtract 241 hundredths from 1200 hundredths.

959 hundredths is \(9.59\).

sections.title: How do I check my change?
sections.label: Change
sections.intro: Prices may have different numbers of displayed digits. Compare and combine them in the same unit before subtracting from the amount paid.

blocks.html: Use pence as whole numbers or keep the decimal points aligned in pounds.

blocks.prompt: A customer pays £25 for a sketchpad costing £2.93 and a pen costing £1.71. Find the change in pounds.
blocks.hint: Combine the prices before subtracting from the amount paid.
blocks.solution:
Add the two prices in pence: 293 p and 171 p.

The total cost is £4.64. Subtract it from £25.

The change is £20.36.

retry.feedback: That is the total cost. Subtract it from the amount handed over.

blocks.html: Add the total and your change. The result should be the amount paid.

igcse-0580-operations-decimal-multiply-d.description: Scale decimals to whole counts and check the size of the result.

sections.title: Where does the decimal point go?
sections.label: Multiply
sections.intro: Represent each factor as an integer count of tenths or hundredths. Multiply those counts and put back the place value of their product.

blocks.html: Tenths times hundredths give thousandths. Powers of ten used in both factors affect the product.

figure.alt: Ten-by-ten grid. Three columns and four rows overlap in twelve squares.
figure.caption: Three tenths of four tenths occupy twelve hundredths of the grid.

blocks.hint: Multiply as integers. Then divide by the scale factors for both numbers.
blocks.solution:
The first factor has 22 tenths. The second has 14 hundredths.

Multiply the integer counts: \(22\times14=308\). Tenths times hundredths give thousandths.

The product is \(0.308\).

blocks.html: The product of two positive decimals below 1 is smaller than either one.

blocks.hint: Multiply as integers. Then divide by the scale factors for both numbers.
blocks.solution:
The first factor has 25 tenths. The second has 17 hundredths.

Multiply the integer counts: \(25\times17=425\). Tenths times hundredths give thousandths.

The product is \(0.425\).

sections.title: How can I make the divisor easier?
sections.label: Divide
sections.intro: A quotient compares two numbers. Multiplying both by an equal non-zero scale leaves the quotient unchanged.

blocks.html: Choose a power of ten that makes the divisor whole.

blocks.hint: Scale both numbers by the same power of ten.
blocks.solution:
Think of the division as \(\frac{0.39}{0.03}\).

Multiply both numbers by 100, so the calculation becomes \(39\div 3\).

The answer is 13. Check that 13 copies of \(0.03\) make \(0.39\).

blocks.html: Scaling only the divisor changes the answer.

blocks.hint: Scale both numbers by the same power of ten.
blocks.solution:
Think of the division as \(\frac{0.96}{0.06}\).

Multiply both numbers by 100, so the calculation becomes \(96\div 6\).

The answer is 16. Check that 16 copies of \(0.06\) make \(0.96\).

sections.title: How do I use a repeated decimal length?
sections.label: Measure
sections.intro: Write the measurements in the same unit. Multiply to find the full amount used, then subtract if the question asks what remains.

blocks.html: Check whether the story asks for one piece, all pieces or the remainder.

blocks.prompt: 7 pieces, each 0.25 m long, are cut from a 3.5 m ribbon. Find the length of ribbon left.
blocks.hint: Multiply the piece length by the number of pieces, then subtract.
blocks.solution:
Find the total removed length by multiplying 7 by \(0.25\).

The pieces use \(1.75\) m. Subtract from the original \(3.5\) m.

The remaining length is \(1.75\) m.

blocks.html: Keep enough precision to finish the exact decimal calculation.

blocks.prompt: 4 pieces, each 0.16 m long, are cut from a 3.8 m ribbon. Find the length of ribbon left.
blocks.hint: Multiply the piece length by the number of pieces, then subtract.
blocks.solution:

The pieces use \(0.64\) m. Subtract from the original \(3.8\) m.

The remaining length is \(3.16\) m.

examples.title: Multiply decimals with different lengths
examples.question: Work out \(1.5\times0.07\) without a calculator.
solution: The first factor has 15 tenths. The second has 7 hundredths.
Multiply the integer counts: \(15\times7=105\). Tenths times hundredths give thousandths.
The product is \(0.105\).

examples.title: Multiply decimals with different lengths

solution: The first factor has 18 tenths. The second has 10 hundredths.

The product is \(0.18\).

examples.question: Work out \(0.3\div0.05\) without a calculator.
solution: Think of the division as \(\frac{0.3}{0.05}\).
Multiply both numbers by 100, so the calculation becomes \(30\div 5\).
The answer is 6. Check that 6 copies of \(0.05\) make \(0.3\).

The remaining length is \(1.72\) m.

igcse-0580-operations-fraction-add-subtr.description: Use equal-sized parts before combining fractions and mixed numbers.

sections.title: Why do the denominators have to match?
sections.label: Equal parts
sections.intro: A denominator tells you the size of the pieces. If two fractions use different sizes, split their bars into equal-size pieces before adding.

blocks.html: Rewrite both fractions with a common denominator. Then add only the counts on top.

figure.alt: Two bars split into six pieces each. Three pieces are marked in one bar and two in the other.
figure.caption: One half is three sixths and one third is two sixths. In sixths the pieces can be combined.

blocks.hint: Rewrite both numbers with the same denominator first.
blocks.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 36.

Write \(\frac{27}{36}+\frac{4}{36}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(\frac{31}{36}\).

retry.feedback: Adding denominators changes the size of a piece. First represent both values in equal-sized parts.

blocks.html: The denominator stays as the common size. Adding the denominators changes the size of every piece.

blocks.hint: Rewrite both numbers with the same denominator first.
blocks.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 7.

Write \(\frac{3}{7}+\frac{4}{7}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(1\).

retry.feedback: Adding denominators changes the size of a piece. First represent both values in equal-sized parts.

sections.title: How do I subtract parts of the same whole?
sections.label: Difference
sections.intro: Draw equal bars to compare what remains. Once the parts match in size, subtract the number of those parts.

blocks.html: Subtract the numerators in the order given. Simplify at the end.

blocks.hint: Rewrite both numbers with the same denominator first.
blocks.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 5.

Write \(\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(0\).

retry.feedback: Adding denominators changes the size of a piece. First represent both values in equal-sized parts.

blocks.html: Check the sign. The result can be negative if you subtract a larger value.

blocks.hint: Rewrite both numbers with the same denominator first.
blocks.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 8.

Write \(\frac{2}{8}-\frac{1}{8}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(\frac{1}{8}\).

retry.feedback: Adding denominators changes the size of a piece. First represent both values in equal-sized parts.

sections.title: What if there is a whole part as well?
sections.label: Mixed
sections.intro: A mixed number has a whole part and a fractional part. Rename each whole in the same-sized pieces before subtracting.

blocks.html: Use one common denominator for both complete numbers.

blocks.hint: Rewrite both numbers with the same denominator first.
blocks.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 6.

Write \(\frac{14}{6}-\frac{3}{6}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(\frac{11}{6}\).

retry.feedback: Adding denominators changes the size of a piece. First represent both values in equal-sized parts.

blocks.html: Keep the value of the whole part when converting to an improper fraction.

blocks.hint: Rewrite both numbers with the same denominator first.
blocks.solution:
The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 45.

Write \(\frac{108}{45}-\frac{10}{45}\). Only change the count on top when combining.

The result simplifies to \(\frac{98}{45}\).

retry.feedback: Adding denominators changes the size of a piece. First represent both values in equal-sized parts.

examples.title: Use equal-sized parts
examples.question: Work out \(\frac{2}{5}+\frac{2}{7}\) without a calculator.
solution: The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 35.
Write \(\frac{14}{35}+\frac{10}{35}\). Only change the count on top when combining.
The result simplifies to \(\frac{24}{35}\).

examples.title: Use equal-sized parts
examples.question: Work out \(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{10}\) without a calculator.
solution: The parts must be the same size. A common denominator is 10.
Write \(\frac{5}{10}+\frac{1}{10}\). Only change the count on top when combining.
The result simplifies to \(\frac{3}{5}\).

examples.title: Use equal-sized parts
examples.question: Work out \(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{8}\) without a calculator.

igcse-0580-operations-fraction-multiply-.description: Find a fraction of a fraction and use the reciprocal when dividing.

sections.title: What is a part of a part?
sections.label: Overlap
sections.intro: Shade some columns of a grid for one fraction and some rows for another. The overlap shows the product as part of the whole.

blocks.html: Multiply the counts on top and the sizes on bottom, then simplify the result.

figure.alt: Twenty cells. Three of five columns and two of four rows overlap in six cells.
figure.caption: The common part covers six of the twenty equal cells.

blocks.hint: Simplify a factor common to a numerator and a denominator if you see one.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators.

Before simplifying, the product is \(\frac{5}{24}\).

If the numerator and denominator share a factor greater than 1, cancel it. The result is \(\frac{5}{24}\).

blocks.html: A product of proper positive fractions should be smaller than its factors.

blocks.hint: Simplify a factor common to a numerator and a denominator if you see one.

sections.title: Why does division use the reciprocal?
sections.label: Reciprocal
sections.intro: Dividing asks how many copies of one number fit into another. If the divisor is a fraction, its reciprocal tells you how many of those pieces make one whole.

blocks.html: Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor. Keep the first fraction the same.

blocks.hint: Invert only the divisor, then multiply.
blocks.solution:
Dividing by the second number is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal \(\frac{9}{4}\).

Use \(\frac{3}{11}\times \frac{9}{4}\). Keep the first fraction in its original order.

The result in simplest form is \(\frac{27}{44}\).

retry.feedback: That multiplies by the divisor. Use its reciprocal instead.

blocks.html: Only invert the second fraction, the number you are dividing by.

blocks.hint: Invert only the divisor, then multiply.
blocks.solution:
Dividing by the second number is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal \(2\).

Use \(\frac{2}{9}\times 2\). Keep the first fraction in its original order.

The result in simplest form is \(\frac{4}{9}\).

retry.feedback: That multiplies by the divisor. Use its reciprocal instead.

sections.title: How do I divide when a number is mixed?
sections.label: Mixed
sections.intro: Rename the whole part and fraction as one improper fraction. Then use the usual division steps.

blocks.html: Convert any mixed number before applying the reciprocal rule.

blocks.hint: Turn the mixed number into an improper fraction, then invert the divisor.
blocks.solution:
Rewrite the whole number and fraction together as \(\frac{17}{4}\).

Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor: \(\frac{17}{4}\times \frac{9}{4}\).

The result is \(\frac{153}{16}\). Convert to a mixed number if the question asks for one.

blocks.html: For written work, use the final fraction or mixed form requested in the question.

blocks.hint: Turn the mixed number into an improper fraction, then invert the divisor.
blocks.solution:

Multiply by the reciprocal of the divisor: \(\frac{23}{7}\times 2\).

The result is \(\frac{46}{7}\). Convert to a mixed number if the question asks for one.

igcse-0580-operations-operation-order.description: Identify each group and work in the order shown by the notation.

sections.title: What should I work out first?
sections.label: Groups
sections.intro: Brackets group a small calculation inside a bigger one. Finish the inner group before applying the operation outside it.

blocks.html: Start inside brackets. Then do powers and roots, products and quotients, and finally sums and differences.

figure.alt: Four levels in order: bracket groups, powers and roots, multiplication or division, then addition or subtraction.
figure.caption: Do each level before moving to the next. Within an equal-priority level, work left to right.

blocks.hint: Finish brackets then multiplication before the outer addition.
blocks.solution:
Calculate the bracket first: 5 plus 2 is 7.

Then multiply 2 by 7 to get 14.

Add 12, giving 26.

retry.feedback: That adds first. The multiplication sits between the bracket and the addition.

blocks.html: Writing the next line one step at a time makes it easier to spot which operation is next.

blocks.hint: Finish brackets then multiplication before the outer addition.
blocks.solution:

Then multiply 5 by 10 to get 50.

Add 15, giving 65.

retry.feedback: That adds first. The multiplication sits between the bracket and the addition.

sections.title: What if the two operations have equal priority?
sections.label: Equal rank
sections.intro: Multiplication and division share one level. Addition and subtraction share another. Within one level, go from left to right.

blocks.html: Treat division and multiplication as equal priority. Start with whichever is earlier in the line.

blocks.hint: On the same level, move left to right.
blocks.solution:
Division and multiplication have equal priority. Read this line from left to right.

Start with \(21\div 7=3\).

Then \(3\times 5=15\).

retry.feedback: This treats the last two numbers as a group. There are no brackets around them.

blocks.html: The order of letters in a mnemonic does not make division always come first.

blocks.hint: On the same level, move left to right.
blocks.solution:

Start with \(10\div 5=2\).

retry.feedback: This treats the last two numbers as a group. There are no brackets around them.

sections.title: Where are the hidden brackets?
sections.label: Fraction bar
sections.intro: A fraction bar groups everything written above it and everything below it. A root bar also shows exactly what goes inside its own operation.

blocks.html: Find the value on top and the value below before dividing.

blocks.hint: Finish the calculation above and below the fraction bar before dividing.
blocks.solution:
The numerator and denominator are separate calculations.

The numerator is 64; the denominator is 4.

Divide to find \(16\).

blocks.html: On a calculator, put brackets around an entire numerator or denominator when using the division key.
